title: What is known about 1RB1RF_1LC0LB_1RE1LD_1RE0LB_1RA0RE_---0RC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RF_1LC0LB_1RE1LD_1RE0LB_1RA0RE_---0RC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The machine is a binary counter that gains 39 or 42 every 8 sweeps. Lean proves that every sweep keeps the counter in its steady form except at a B-overflow (once every second doubling), so a halt would have to come out of a B-overflow transient; the run through the first one is evaluated too. A dedicated pass decoded the transient completely: for about 3·2w bounces the binary counter runs against a base-3 counter written over the long block, and then a short clean-up loop has to bring the block back to zeros. The digits the transient leaves behind depend on the width in a number-theoretic way, the block is not safe under arbitrary orders of operations, and one digit pattern makes the clean-up long. So the missing lemma is not a routine induction. An exact accelerated simulation shows 16 transients (to 1.1·1017 steps) all recovering, with no halt.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: Where a halt can come from
claims.text: If the machine halts on its third step from a configuration, that configuration is one of: E with 0 under the head, 1 right, 0 two right. So a run can reach a halt only through one of these patterns, and a proof that the machine never halts only has to rule them out. The proof splits on the state and the five cells around the head.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 63,134 cells have been visited and 32,679 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.514).

claims.title: Tape structure
claims.text: At 108 steps the tape ends in (0111)^3998 011 A>1 (1001)^907 1, at 109 in (1011)^1088 10 B>1 (0110)^14656 011: two long periodic blocks meet at the head and trade length, with an irregular region of short words to their left that changes slowly.

claims.title: The two sweeps across the long block
claims.text: L (1011)^n 1 0 C> 0^inf reaches L C> 1 (1001)^n 10011 0^inf in 4n+8 steps, and L 1 F> (1001)^n 10011 0^inf reaches L 1 (0111)^n 01110 C> 0^inf in 4n+5 steps, for all n and every tape L.

claims.title: Every sweep that does not overflow the counter
claims.text: The middle part of each visit (between the two block crossings) is proved for all 7 shallow cases (inner counter i < 7, i → i+1) and all 162 deep cases (i = 7: V → V + 39 or 42, t flips), for every value of the five low digits, digit 5 when it matters, and a carry crossing any number of 1-digits, for every tape left of the digit that stops the carry. With back/forth these cover every visit that does not overflow V.

claims.title: The counter model holds for 2·10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: c/visits.c parses every visit (head in state C on the blank cell right of the tape) as [1] U(b_top)..U(b_1) b_0 0 1 M(t) I(i) (1011)^m 1 0 and checks each pair of consecutive visits against the rule; 70,664 visits, 0 exceptions; 5 A-overflows and 4 B-overflow transients (8-32 visits each) all behave as described in the README.

claims.title: The A-overflows
claims.text: A deep visit in phase A whose carry runs through all digits to the blank tape (0^inf (U(1))^(k+1) [U(b5)] low M(t) I(7)) ends as phase B with the same width and a lone 1 in front (0^inf 1 (U(0))^(k+1) [U(b5)] low' M(1-t) I(0)), for all 81 cases and every k.

claims.title: Every steady visit that is not a B-overflow leads to a steady visit
claims.text: The visit configurations are written with the digits of V as a list of bits; Steady says the tape has the steady layout (phase A or B, at least 7 digits, block at least as long as the counter is wide). For every such configuration that is not a B-overflow, the run reaches another steady configuration: shallow visits, deep visits with a carry through any number of 1-digits, and A-overflows, for every counter value, width and block length.

claims.title: A halt can only come in a B-overflow transient, and not in the first one
claims.text: The run from blank tape reaches a steady visit (visit 280, step 1,882,602, evaluated), so with steady_step a halt needs the run to reach a steady B-overflow visit first; the run through the first B-overflow transient to visit 2688 (step 31,879,658) is evaluated too, so that B-overflow must come at step 31,879,658 or later.

claims.title: Non-halting follows from one lemma about the B-overflows
claims.text: If every steady B-overflow visit is followed by a steady visit, the machine never halts from blank tape.

claims.title: Every B-overflow transient up to its exit sweep
claims.text: The symbolic simulator runs all 81 possible B-overflows (switch t, five low digits, digit 5 when they carry) for any number of digits and any block length: 0 to 48 ordinary-looking transient sweeps, in which a small counter written into M is incremented instead of V, and then the exit sweep, where it stops because an inner counter carries into the zero digits.

claims.title: The transient decoded: the odometer
claims.text: Cut the tape at the first cell of M (the seam). Left of it is a binary counter L in 3-cell words that gains 1 at every bounce and has four phases; the head leaves it in state A (steady sweeps) or, between the overflows of phases B and B', in state E (the transient). The next 63 cells are a finite control with four base-3 digits; the block is a base-3 counter in 4-cell digits (0110 = 0, 0010 = 1, 1110 = 2), and a visit is the operation ‘E-send’ on an all-zero block. Checked by exact simulation: c/odo.c relies on this layout to skip the walks over zero digits, falls back to plain steps if it is ever violated, and reports 0 violations in 1.1·1017 steps.

claims.title: The left counter of the odometer
claims.text: For any row of 3-cell words and any tape to the right: entering in state B or D, the head turns the nearest word 0 behind j words 1 into a word 1, rewrites the j words as 1, 0, 1, 0, … and leaves in state A (j even) or E (j odd) after 6j + 5 steps; with no word 0 a new one is added on the blank tape. The four phase overflows (A → B → A' → B' → A with one more digit) follow for every width, with the state in which the head leaves: E exactly for B → A' and A' → B'.

claims.title: No halt in 1.1·10<sup>17</sup> steps; 16 transients recover
claims.text: c/odo.c runs the machine from blank tape, skipping only the head's walk over the zero digits of the block (restored unchanged on the way back; otherwise it falls back to single steps). Its tape agrees with the plain simulation at 223 checkpoints up to 3·109 steps. To 1.1·1017 steps (165,831,169 visits): no halt; 16 B-overflow transients (widths 13 to 28), each back at a steady visit after a clean-up of 123 to 366 bounces. The block digits left by the transients (2122102, 10220111, 10221222, …) show no pattern.

claims.title: Why no regular invariant works: the block is unsafe under free sends
claims.text: Taken alone, the block misbehaves under some orders of its two operations: from an all-zero block the sends A, E, A, A, A, E, A, A, E make the head come back in state C instead of B or D (direct simulation). The real run avoids such orders by the timing of the window's counters, so a proof has to carry the exact relation between window and block; closed regular tape languages (CTL, n-gram CPS) cannot.

claims.title: A digit pattern that makes the clean-up long
claims.text: The clean-up divides the block's value by 3 at each send (plus 4 when the remainder is 2), and 5 = digits 2, 1 is a fixed point: started with 2 1 in the two lowest places, the pattern travels one word per send to the far end of the block, about 5 bounces per block word instead of a few hundred in total (492 bounces for a block of 93 words, 1,182 for 233, in synthetic starts at width 9, which still recovered). It did not occur in the 16 transients seen; what it does at real sizes, where the block length is of the order of the binary counter's remaining room, is not known.
claims.where: README (Why the remaining lemma is hard), c/seam.c

claims.title: No verdict from heuristics
claims.text: Earlier versions of this page said the machine almost certainly never halts. That is withdrawn: 16 transients recover and no halt is in sight, but every transient leaves different base-3 digits on the block, a naive model gives the long-clean-up pattern a density of about 1/9, and nothing is known about what happens then at large widths.

claims.title: Regular-language deciders tried (F11)
claims.text: None of these closes: each reaches a halting configuration in its abstraction, which says nothing about whether the machine halts. n-gram CPS (tools/c/ngramcps.c), equal widths on both sides: a halting local configuration is reached with plain up to width 18, history 1 up to width 14, history 2 up to width 13, history 3 up to width 11, LRU history up to width 13 (larger widths ran out of the 150 s or 60 million configuration budget). n-gram CPS with every cell tagged by its position mod p: fails for p = 2 up to width 16, p = 3 up to width 20, p = 4 up to width 20, p = 6 up to width 20. Run-length windows (the K nearest runs of equal macro cells on each side, run lengths kept exactly below T and mod M above): fails for all 72 parameter sets (cells of 1 to 4 bits, K = 2, 4, 6, T = 2, 4, M = 1, 2, 4). Two-automaton closed tape language by SAT (a deterministic automaton reading each side inward, n states each, CaDiCaL): no solution for n = 2..8; n = 9 not finished in 150 s.
claims.where: sweeps of 13 November 2026 (family F11); the tagged and run-length deciders are not in the repository yet

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not proved. Missing: the hypothesis of nonhalting_of_transients, that every B-overflow transient ends at a steady visit. A proof needs the E-mode loop as an exact base-3 count over about 2w rounds for general w, the block language of the clean-up loop including the travelling pattern, and the arithmetic that the clean-up ends before the binary counter's next overflow; or else a width at which it fails. See Next steps in the README.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has been followed for 1.1·10<sup>17</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: Proved in Lean: a halt can only happen inside a B-overflow transient (once per two doublings of the counter), and not in the first one.
No halt in an exact accelerated simulation; 16 transients, all recovered.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: A counter that counts by 81 every 16 sweeps
html: The head sweeps from one end of the tape to the other and back. Look at the tape each time the head arrives at the right end (a visit): it always has the same layout.

<svg viewBox='0 0 560 96' role='img' aria-label='the tape at a visit: lone 1, the digits of V, M(t), I(i), the long block, the head' style='width:100%;max-width:560px;height:auto;font:12px var(--mono)'><rect x='10' y='20' width='14' height='26' fill='var(--muted)'/><rect x='24' y='20' width='150' height='26' fill='var(--head)'/><text x='99' y='37' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>digits of V</text><rect x='174' y='20' width='70' height='26' fill='var(--accent)'/><text x='209' y='37' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>M(t)</text><rect x='244' y='20' width='46' height='26' fill='var(--fg2)'/><text x='267' y='37' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>I(i)</text><rect x='290' y='20' width='240' height='26' fill='var(--ink)'/><text x='410' y='37' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>(1011)^m, +1 copy per sweep</text><text x='540' y='37' fill='var(--fg2)'>C</text><text x='99' y='66' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg2)'>+39 or +42</text><text x='99' y='82' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>every 8 sweeps</text><text x='209' y='66' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg2)'>t flips</text><text x='267' y='66' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg2)'>i+1 mod 8</text><text x='10' y='14' fill='var(--muted)'>phase B only</text></svg>

• At the left, a number V written in binary, one digit per 6 cells (b01101, where b is the digit).
  • Then a fixed 45-cell word M(t) with one switch cell t, and a 3-digit counter i written the same way.
  • Then the long block (1011)^m, one copy longer at each visit.

At each visit i goes up by one. When it wraps from 7 to 0, the head walks all the way into V and adds 39 to it (if t = 0) or 42 (if t = 1), and t flips. So V grows by 81 every 16 visits, carries ripple left exactly as when you add on paper.

Overflows

When V runs out of digits something special happens. The first time (phase A to phase B), the digits are rewritten one cell to the right with a lone 1 in front. The second time (a B-overflow, phase B to phase A), after a transient of up to 48 visits and one very long sweep, V has one more digit. Each such cycle takes twice as long as the previous one, so the left end of the tape grows only like the logarithm of the time.

sections.heading: Everything except one kind of overflow
html: Each sweep is cut into three pieces: crossing the block leftwards, the turn-around in M, I and the low digits of V, and crossing the block back. The two crossings are proved in Lean for blocks of any length. The turn-around is proved in 250 separate theorems: 7 for the ordinary visits (i < 7), 162 for the adding visits (one for each value of the five lowest digits of V, the switch t, and whether a carry goes further, which also covers carries running through any number of 1-digits), and 81 for the first kind of overflow, where the carry runs off the left end of the counter.

Then the pieces are glued together. A predicate Steady describes the tape at a visit: the digits of V as a list of bits, M, I and the block. One theorem, steady_step, says: from any steady visit the machine gets to another steady visit, unless the visit starts the second kind of overflow (a B-overflow). It is proved by looking at the low digits and at the first 0-digit above them, and picking the right one of the 250 theorems. The start from blank tape to the first steady visit (1,882,602 steps) is computed.

Proved: if the machine ever halts, it does so inside a B-overflow, and not inside the first one (at step 30 million, also computed in Lean). Proved: if every B-overflow ends in a steady visit again, the machine never halts.
So the whole question comes down to the B-overflows. They are rare (the counter must double twice between two of them) but complicated, see the next section.

sections.heading: The B-overflow: an odometer with two kinds of wheels
html: There is a second way to read the tape that also works during the overflow. Cut it at one fixed cell, the seam. Left of the seam is a binary counter that goes up by one every time the head bounces off it. Right of the seam, after 63 cells of machinery, the long block is a counter too, but in base 3: each group of four cells is one digit.

<svg viewBox='0 0 560 120' role='img' aria-label='the tape cut at the seam: binary counter L, window of 63 cells, block of base-3 digits' style='width:100%;max-width:560px;height:auto;font:12px var(--mono)'><rect x='10' y='30' width='150' height='28' fill='var(--head)'/><text x='85' y='48' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>binary counter L</text><line x1='162' y1='20' x2='162' y2='68' stroke='var(--fg)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='162' y='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg)'>seam</text><rect x='164' y='30' width='90' height='28' fill='none' stroke='var(--fg)'/><text x='209' y='48' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg)'>window</text><rect x='256' y='30' width='290' height='28' fill='var(--muted)'/><text x='401' y='48' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>block: base-3 digits, mostly 0</text><text x='85' y='78' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg)'>+1 per bounce</text><text x='209' y='78' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg)'>81-step cycle</text><text x='401' y='78' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg)'>+1 word per visit</text><text x='280' y='106' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg)'>normal sweeps: the head leaves L in state A · transient: in state E</text></svg>

In normal times the block holds only zeros, and a sweep to the right end and back just appends one more zero: that is the simple rule above. The binary counter is written in a redundant way with four phases. During one stretch out of four (the B-overflow transient, about 3·2w bounces when the counter has w digits) it sends the head back in a different state, and then the window stops making sweeps and instead counts in base 3, pushing its carries into the block. When the stretch ends, the low digits of the block hold a base-3 number that depends on 2w: 2122102 at w = 13, 10220111 at w = 14, 10221222 at w = 15, and so on, with no visible pattern.

Then a clean-up loop wipes these digits: each pass divides the number by 3, more or less. In the 16 transients followed so far (up to 1.1·1017 steps) it took between 123 and 366 bounces, and the machine was back to normal sweeps with a counter one digit longer.

Why this is not a proof. Three things stand in the way. First, the block alone is fragile: fed its two operations in the wrong order (nine operations are enough) it sends the head back in a state the rest of the tape is not prepared for. The real machine never uses that order, but only because of how its counters are timed, so the proof must track the timing exactly. Second, the digits left on the block are a question about powers of 2 written in base 3, the kind of question (as in Collatz-like problems) for which no general method is known. Third, one particular pair of digits (a 2 followed by a 1 in the lowest places) is a fixed point of the clean-up: instead of vanishing it travels along the whole block, and the clean-up takes about five bounces per block word instead of a few hundred in all. That has not happened yet. If it happens at a large width, nobody knows whether the machine recovers.
So the honest summary is: the machine is fully understood as a mechanism, it has survived 16 of its dangerous moments, and whether it survives all of them is open.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.514).
After 109 steps the tape spans 63,134 cells (82 left of the start, 46,087 right), with a density of 1s of 0.518.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

  • 1RB0LD_1RC0RB_1RD1RF_1LE0LD_1RB1LA_---0RE: rename A→C, B→D, C→E, D→A, E→B, F→F; it is this table started in state D

summary: A binary counter at the left end (+39 or +42 every 8 sweeps) facing a base-3 counter written over the growing block; Lean proves a halt can only come in a B-overflow transient (not the first); the transient is now fully decoded and followed exactly to 1.1*10^17 steps (16 transients, no halt), but its end state depends number-theoretically on the width and the proof that it always recovers is missing: open.
family: odometer: binary counter (+39/+42 per 8 sweeps) against a base-3 block counter
